<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">
interruption of our program could occur for a variety of reasons, including: (1)&nbsp;adverse changes in laws or regulations affecting our primary insurer or AssuranceOne; (2)&nbsp;a change in
the financial condition or financial strength ratings of our primary insurer or AssuranceOne; (3)&nbsp;negative developments in the loss reserves or future loss experience of AssuranceOne, which render it uneconomical for us to continue the program;
(4)&nbsp;termination or expiration of the reinsurance agreement with our primary insurer, coupled with an inability by us to identify quickly and negotiate an acceptable arrangement with a replacement carrier; or (5)&nbsp;competitive factors in the
property insurance market. If there is a termination or interruption of this program or if fewer small business customers elected to satisfy their insurance obligations through our program, we would experience lower revenues and our net income may
be reduced. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Our financial statements are based in part on assumptions and estimates made by our management that could vary from actual results.
</I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Pursuant to accounting principles generally accepted in the United States, we utilize certain assumptions and estimates in
preparing our financial statements, including but not limited to, when accounting for income recognition, the allowance for credit losses, the residual values of leased equipment, deferred initial direct costs and fees, late fee receivables, the
fair value of financial instruments, estimated losses from insurance program, and income taxes. If the assumptions or estimates underlying our financial statements are incorrect, we may experience significant losses as the ultimate realization of
value may be materially different than the amounts reflected in our consolidated statement of financial position as of any particular date. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Specific to our allowance for credit losses, in connection with our financing activities, we record an allowance to provide for estimated
losses based on both qualitative and quantitative factors including, among other things, past collection experience, lease and loan delinquency data, industry data, economic conditions and our assessment of collection risks. Significant management
judgment is required to determine the appropriate level of the allowance and, therefore, our determination of this allowance may prove to be inadequate to cover losses in connection with our portfolio of leases and loans. Factors that could lead to
the inadequacy of our allowance may include our inability to manage collections effectively, unanticipated adverse changes in the economy or discrete events adversely affecting specific leasing customers, industries or geographic areas. Losses in
excess of our allowance for credit losses would cause us to increase our provision for credit losses, reducing or eliminating our operating income. On January&nbsp;1, 2020, the Company adopted the guidance of ASU
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">2016-13,</FONT><I>&nbsp;Financial Instruments&#151;Credit Losses (Topic 326): Measurement of Credit Losses on Financial Instruments</I> (&#147;CECL&#148;) to measure its allowance for credit losses. This standard
substantially replaced the prior measurement that was based on probable, incurred losses. Starting in 2020, the recognized allowance estimate will include expected credit losses over the remaining contractual term of the existing portfolio. After
the adoption of this standard, our allowance estimate will continue to involve management&#146;s judgment, and assessment of various qualitative and quantitative factors, and such estimate will still be subject to continual update driven by similar
factors outlined above. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Specific to our estimates of residual value of equipment, we record sales-type financing leases at the aggregate
future minimum lease payments plus the estimated residual value less unearned income. Residual values are established on our balance sheet at lease inception based on our estimate of the expected fair value of the equipment at the end of the lease
term. Realization of residual values depends on numerous factors including: the general market conditions at the time of expiration of the lease; the customer&#146;s election to enter into a renewal period; the cost of comparable new equipment; the
obsolescence of the leased equipment; any unusual or excessive wear and tear on or damage to the equipment; the effect of any additional or amended government regulations; and the foreclosure by a secured party of our interest in a defaulted lease.
Our failure to realize our recorded residual values would reduce the residual value of equipment recorded as assets on our balance sheet and may reduce our operating income. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">For additional information on the key areas for which assumptions and estimates are used in preparing our financial statements, see &#147;Part
II&#151;Item 7. Management&#146;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>If we experience significant telecommunications or technology downtime, our operations would be disrupted and our ability to generate operating income
could be negatively impacted.</I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our business depends in large part on our telecommunications and information management systems. The
temporary or permanent loss of our computer systems, telecommunications equipment or software systems, through casualty or operating malfunction, could disrupt our originations and operations and negatively impact our ability to secure new business
and to service our customers. This could lead to significant declines in our operating income. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I></I><B><I>A failure in or breach of our technology
infrastructure or information protection programs, or those of our outsource service providers, could result in the inadvertent disclosure of the confidential information of our customers and affiliates or confidential personal information of
personal guarantors of our loans and leases. Any such failure, including as a result of cyber-attacks against us or our outsource partners, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-compliance</FONT> with our contractual or other legal obligations
regarding such information, or a violation of the Company&#146;s privacy and security policies with respect to such information, could adversely affect us</I></B><I>. </I></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our business model and our reputation as a service provider to our clients are dependent upon our ability to safeguard confidential
information. Although we have put in place, and require our outsource service providers to follow, a comprehensive information security program that we monitor and update as needed, security breaches could occur through intentional or unintentional
acts by individuals having authorized or unauthorized access to confidential information of our customers, employees or stakeholders which could potentially compromise confidential information processed and stored in or transmitted through our
technology infrastructure. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The legal, regulatory and contractual environment surrounding information security and privacy is constantly
evolving and companies that collect and retain such information are under increasing attack by cyber-criminals around the world. A significant actual or potential theft, loss, fraudulent use or misuse of customer, stockholder, employee or our data
by cybercrime or otherwise, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-compliance</FONT> with our contractual or other legal obligations regarding such data or a violation of our privacy and security policies with respect to such data could adversely
impact our reputation and could result in significant costs, fines, litigation or regulatory action against us. Increasingly, our products and services are accessed through the Internet, and security breaches in connection with the delivery of our
services via the Internet may affect us and could be detrimental to our reputation, business, operating results and financial condition. We cannot be certain that advances in criminal capabilities, new discoveries in the field of cryptography or
other developments will not compromise or breach the technology protecting the networks that access our products and services. </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">It is possible that in some future quarter our operating results may be below the expectations of financial market analysts and investors and,
as a result of these and other factors, the price of our common stock may decline. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>We have historically returned capital to shareholders through
normal dividends, special dividends and share repurchases. There can be no assurances that these forms of capital returns are the optimal use of our capital or that they will continue into the future. </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">During 2019, our Board of Directors authorized an updated share repurchase program. These repurchases reduced our market capitalization and
public float, which is the number of shares of our common stock that are owned by <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-affiliated</FONT> stockholders and available for trading in the securities markets, which may reduce the volume of trading in our
shares and result in reduced liquidity and volatility in our stock price. The market price of our common stock has been and may continue to be volatile which may affect your ability to sell our common stock at an advantageous price. For example, the
closing market price of our common stock on the NASDAQ fluctuated between $19.88 per share and $24.84 per share during 2019 and may continue to fluctuate. Market price fluctuations in our common stock may be due to factors both within and outside of
our control, including our strategic actions, industry and regulatory matters or other material public announcements, as well as a variety of additional factors including, without limitation, those set forth under these &#147;Risk Factors&#148; and
&#147;Cautionary Note Regarding Forward-Looking Statements.&#148; </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In August 2019, our Board of Directors provided a new authorization for
up to $10&nbsp;million of share repurchases, and as of December&nbsp;31, 2019, we have $8.9&nbsp;million of share repurchase authorization remaining. We have no obligation to repurchase shares under this authorization, and any share repurchase
program may be extended, modified, suspended or discontinued at any time. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Any repurchases would utilize cash that we will not be able to
use in other ways, or to meet other potential demands, and may not prove to be the best use of our capital. There can be no assurance that we will repurchase any, or the full amount authorized under any share repurchase program, or that any past or
future repurchases will have a positive impact on our stock price. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Future sales of our Common Stock by our significant shareholders may depress our
stock price or impair our ability to raise funds in new share offerings. Our existing shareholders may be able to exert significant influence over matters requiring shareholder approval and over our management. </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">A small number of shareholders own a substantial amount of our Common Stock. As of December&nbsp;31, 2019, our top 5 largest shareholders
beneficially own 54% of our common stock. The market price of our common stock could be adversely affected as a result of sales of a large number of our common stock shares in the market, </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We are a Pennsylvania corporation. Anti-takeover provisions of Pennsylvania law could make it more difficult for a third party to acquire

<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Dividend Policy </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">On October&nbsp;31,

<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Federal Reserve Board has issued policy statements which provide that, as a general matter, insured banks and bank holding companies

also depend upon our earnings, financial condition, capital requirements, cash flow, long-range plans and such other factors as our Board of Directors may deem relevant. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Number of Record Holders </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">There were 164
holders of record of our common stock at February&nbsp;28, 2020. We believe that the number of beneficial owners is greater than the number of record holders because a large portion of our common stock is held of record through brokerage firms in

such amounts as market conditions warrant. Any shares purchased under this plan are returned to the status of authorized but unissued shares of common stock. The repurchases may be made on the open market, in block trades or otherwise. Any stock
repurchase programs do not obligate the Company to acquire any particular amount of common stock, and such programs may be suspended at any time at the Company&#146;s discretion. The repurchases are funded using the Company&#146;s working capital.
</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In addition to the repurchases described above, pursuant to the Company&#146;s 2003 Equity Compensation Plan, as amended (the &#147;2003
Plan&#148;) and the Company&#146;s 2014 Equity Compensation Plan (approved by the Company&#146;s shareholders on June&nbsp;3, 2014) (the &#147;2014 Plan&#148;) and the Company&#146;s 2019 Equity Compensation Plan (approved by the Company&#146;s
shareholders on May&nbsp;30, 2019) (the &#147;2019 Plan&#148; and, together with the 2014 Plan and the 2003 Plan, the &#147;Equity Compensation Plans&#148;), participants may have shares withheld to cover income taxes. There were 22,741 shares
repurchased to cover income tax withholding in connection with shares granted under the Equity Plans during the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 at an average <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">per-share</FONT> cost of $22.85. </P>

Services Corp. and its subsidiaries. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Overview </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Founded in 1997, we are a nationwide provider of credit products and services to small and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">mid-sized</FONT>
businesses. The products and services we provide to our customers include loans and leases for the acquisition of commercial equipment (including Commercial Vehicle Group (&#147;CVG&#148;) assets) and working capital loans. In May 2000, we
established AssuranceOne, Ltd., a Bermuda-based, wholly-owned captive insurance subsidiary (&#147;Assurance One&#148;), which enables us to reinsure the property insurance coverage for the equipment financed by Marlin Leasing Corporation
(&#147;MLC&#148;) and Marlin Business Bank (&#147;MBB&#148;) for our&nbsp;small business customers. In 2008, we opened MBB, a commercial bank chartered by the State of Utah and a member of the Federal Reserve System. MBB serves as the Company&#146;s
primary funding source through its issuance of Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (&#147;FDIC&#148;)-insured deposits. In January 2017, we completed the acquisition of Horizon Keystone Financial (&#147;HKF&#148;), an equipment leasing company
which primarily identifies and sources lease and loan contracts for investor partners for a fee, and in September 2018, we completed the acquisition of Fleet Financing Resources (&#147;FFR&#148;), an company specializing in the leasing and financing
of both new and used commercial vehicles, with an emphasis on livery equipment and other types of commercial vehicles used by small businesses.</P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">-33- </P>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We are continuing to execute on our objective to transition from a micro-ticket equipment
lessor into a nationwide provider of capital solutions to small businesses. This includes the following priorities: a focus on strategically expanding our target market; better leveraging our capital and fixed cost base through origination and
portfolio growth, improving our operating efficiency, and proactively managing our risk profile. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We access our end user customers
primarily through origination sources consisting of independent commercial equipment dealers, various national account programs, through direct solicitation of our end user customers and through relationships with select lease and loan brokers. We
use both a telephonic direct sales model and, for strategic larger accounts, outside sales executives to market to our origination sources and end user customers. Through these origination sources, we are able to cost-effectively access end user
customers while also helping our origination sources obtain financing for their customers. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">At December&nbsp;31, 2019, we had
$1.2&nbsp;billion in total assets, substantially comprised of our net investment in leases and loans which totaled $1.0&nbsp;billion. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our
leases are fixed-rate transactions with terms generally ranging from 36 to 72&nbsp;months. At December&nbsp;31, 2019, our equipment finance lease and loan portfolio consisted of approximately 91,000 accounts, excluding Working Capital Loans, with an
average original term of 49 months and average original transaction size of approximately $16,000. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">MBB offers a flexible loan program
called Working Capital Loans. Working Capital Loans is tailored to the small business market to provide customers access to capital to help grow their businesses. As of December&nbsp;31, 2019, we had approximately $ 60.9&nbsp;million, not including
the allowance for credit losses allocated to loans of $1.9&nbsp;million, of small business loans on the balance sheet.&nbsp;Generally, these loans range from $5,000 to $150,000, have flexible 6 to 24 month terms, and have automated daily and weekly
payback. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our revenue consists of interest and fees from our leases and loans and, to a lesser extent, income from our property insurance
program and other fee income. Our expenses consist of interest expense and operating expenses, which include salaries and benefits and other general and administrative expenses. As a credit lender, our earnings are also impacted by credit losses.
For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, our net credit losses were 2.18% of our average total finance receivables. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We recognize
interest income over the term of our leases, as our leases are classified as sales-type leases. The net investment in sales-type leases recognized on our balance sheets consists of the sum of total minimum lease payments receivable and the estimated
residual value of leased equipment, less unearned lease income. Unearned lease income consists of the excess of the total future minimum lease payments receivable plus the estimated residual value expected to be realized at the end of the lease term
plus deferred net initial direct costs and fees less the cost of the related equipment. Approximately 55% of our lease portfolio at December&nbsp;31, 2019 amortizes over the lease term to a $1 residual value. For the remainder of the portfolio, we
must estimate end of term residual values for the leased assets. Failure to correctly estimate residual values could result in losses being realized on the disposition of the equipment at the end of the lease term. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We fund our business primarily through the issuance of fixed-rate FDIC-insured deposits and money market demand accounts raised nationally by
MBB, as well as, from time to time, fixed-rate asset backed securitization transactions. We anticipate that FDIC-insured deposits issued by MBB will continue to represent our primary source of funds for the foreseeable future. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Stock Repurchase Plan </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">During the year
ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, we purchased 294,686 total shares of our common stock in the open market at an average cost of $23.09 under the 2019 and 2017 Repurchase Plans. At December&nbsp;31, 2019, $8.9&nbsp;million of authorizations remain under
the 2019 Repurchase Plan. This authority may be exercised from </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">-34- </P>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">
time to time and in such amounts as market conditions warrant. The stock repurchase program does not obligate us to acquire any particular amount of common stock, and it may be suspended at any
time at our discretion. Stock repurchases are funded using our working capital. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Adoption of accounting change for credit losses effective in
2020&#151;&#147;CECL&#148; </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Effective January&nbsp;1, 2020, we adopted new guidance for accounting for our allowance, or ASU <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">2016-13,</FONT><I>&nbsp;Financial Instruments&#151;Credit Losses (Topic 326): Measurement of Credit Losses on Financial Instruments</I> (&#147;CECL&#148;). CECL replaces the probable/ incurred loss model that we
historically used to measure our allowance, with a measurement of expected credit losses for the contractual term of our current portfolio of loans and leases. Under CECL, an allowance, or estimate of credit losses, will be recognized immediately
upon the origination of a loan or lease, and will be adjusted in each subsequent reporting period. This estimate of credit losses takes into consideration all remaining cashflows the Company expects to receive or derive from the pools of contracts,
including recoveries after <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">charge-off,</FONT> and certain future cashflows from residual assets. The provision for credit losses recognized in our Consolidated statements of operations under CECL, starting in 2020,
will be primarily driven by origination volumes, offset by the reversal of the allowance for any contracts sold, plus adjustments for changes in estimate each subsequent reporting period, including adjustments for economic forecasts within a
reasonable and supportable time period. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">While CECL requires us to measure our current estimate of expected credit losses over the
remaining life of all contracts currently in the portfolio, such measurement remains an estimate, is inherently uncertain, and is subject to update. Changes in economic conditions, the risk characteristics and composition of the portfolio, default
and recovery trends, bankruptcy laws, and estimated cash flows associated with residual activity, among other factors, may drive changes in modeled assumptions, may cause management to adjust the allowance estimate through qualitative adjustments
and/or may result in actual losses that vary from of our current estimate. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The adoption of this standard is expected to result in
approximately an $11&nbsp;million increase to our allowance, with offsetting entries to deferred taxes and retained earnings. For regulatory capital, we will avail ourselves of the option to phase in over a period of three years the day one effects
of CECL and expects to continue to be well capitalized under the Basel III regulatory framework after the adoption of this standard. The <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">phase-in</FONT> will be straight-line over the three-year period such that we
will phase in 25&nbsp;percent of the transitional amounts in the first year, and an additional 25% over each of the next two years so that we would have phased in 75&nbsp;percent of the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">day-one</FONT> effects during
year three. At the beginning of the fourth year, we would have completely reflected in regulatory capital the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">day-one</FONT> effects of CECL. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">See further discussion in Note 2, Summary of Significant Accounting Policies. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>RESULTS OF OPERATIONS </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Comparison of the Years
Ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 and 2018 </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Net income</I></B><I>.</I> Net income of $27.1&nbsp;million was reported for the year
ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, resulting in diluted earnings per share of $2.20, compared to net income of $25.0&nbsp;million and diluted earnings per share of $2.00 for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Return on average assets was 2.18% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, compared to a return of 2.29% for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2018. Return on average equity was 13.33% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, compared to a return of 13.27% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Overall, our average net investment in total finance receivables for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 increased 8.9% to
$1,028.6&nbsp;million, compared to $944.6&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. This change was primarily due to origination volume continuing to exceed lease and loan repayments, asset sales and charge-offs. The <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">end-of-period</FONT></FONT> net investment in total finance receivables at December&nbsp;31, 2019 was $1,006.5&nbsp;million, an increase of 0.6% from $1,000.7&nbsp;million at
December&nbsp;31, 2018. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">-35- </P>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">During the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, we generated 31,246 new leases and loans in
the amount of $801.9&nbsp;million, compared to 33,105 new leases and loans in the amount of $704.9&nbsp;million originated for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. Approval rates decreased from 57% at December&nbsp;31, 2018 to 55% at
December&nbsp;31, 2019. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 compared to the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, net interest and fee
income increased $2.1&nbsp;million, or 2.2%, primarily due to a $10.4&nbsp;million increase in interest income and a $0.6&nbsp;million increase in fee income offset by a $7.6&nbsp;million increase in interest expense. The provision for credit losses
increased $8.5&nbsp;million, or 43.6%, to $28.0&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 from $19.5&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, primarily due to higher charge-offs attributed to increased delinquencies in
the second half of 2019 as well as the growth in average finance receivables and charge-offs in the fourth quarter of $0.9&nbsp;million due to fraudulent activity by a single vendor partner. Gain on sale of leases and loans increased
$13.8&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 compared to the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 due to increased syndication volumes. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">-36- </P>

</DIV></Center>

<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Net interest and fee income increased $2.1&nbsp;million, or 2.2%, to $97.6&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 from
$95.5&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. The net interest and fee margin was 9.49% and 10.11% for the years ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 and December&nbsp;31, 2018, respectively. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Interest income, net of amortized initial direct costs and fees, increased $10.4&nbsp;million, or 10.7%, to $107.4&nbsp;million for the year
ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 from $97.0&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. The increase in interest income was principally due to a 8.9% increase in average total finance receivables, which increased $84.0&nbsp;million to
$1,028.6&nbsp;million at December&nbsp;31, 2019 from $944.6&nbsp;million at December&nbsp;31, 2018. The increase in average total finance receivables was primarily due to origination volume continuing to exceed lease and loan repayments, asset sales
and charge-offs. The weighted average implicit interest rate on new finance receivables increased 47 basis point to 12.86% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, from 12.45% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Fee income decreased $0.6&nbsp;million, or 3.8%, to $15.2&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 from $15.8&nbsp;million for
the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. Fee income included approximately $8.4&nbsp;million in late fee income for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, which decreased 9.7%, compared to $9.3&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018.
Fee income also included approximately $3.7&nbsp;million of net residual income the years ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 and 2018. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Fee
income, as a percentage of average total finance receivables, decreased 20 basis points to 1.48% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 from 1.68% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. Late fees remained the largest component of fee income
at 0.82% as a percentage of average total finance receivables for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, compared to 0.99% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. As a percentage of average total finance receivables, net residual income was 0.36%
for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, compared to 0.40% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Interest expense increased

<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Gain on Sale of Leases and Loans.</I></B><I> </I>Gain on sale of leases and loans increased $13.8&nbsp;million to $22.2&nbsp;million for
the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, from $8.4&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. Assets sold grew to $310.4&nbsp;million, for 2019 compared to $139.0&nbsp;million for 2018. We rely on the sale of finance receivables to third
parties in the capital markets as an important source of our liquidity, and use such sales to manage the size and composition of our balance sheet and capital levels. Our sales execution decisions, including the timing, volume and frequency of such
sales, depend on many factors including our origination volumes, the characteristics of our contracts versus market requirements, our current assessment of our balance sheet composition and capital levels, and current market conditions, among other
factors. The execution of such sales results in the derecognition of the lease and loan assets, and the recognition of a gain (or loss) and the servicing asset and liability as applicable on the sale date driven by the pricing and net proceeds
received; the immediate recognition of such gain is in exchange for all future revenues from the contracts and the transfer all risk of loss for sales without recourse and substantially all risks of loss for sales with recourse. Substantially all of
our asset sales to date have been without recourse. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Insurance premiums written and earned.</I></B><I> </I>Insurance premiums
written and earned increased $0.7&nbsp;million to $8.8&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 from $8.1&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, primarily due to an increase in the number of contracts enrolled in the
insurance program as well as higher average ticket size. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Other income.</I></B> Other income increased $8.0&nbsp;million to
$13.0&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 from $5.0&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. A significant component of the increase in other income is property tax income that was previously netted against property
tax expense for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, but is presented as a separate component of revenue for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, as a result of the adoption of ASU <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">2016-02</FONT> and related
ASUs. Selected major components of other income for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 included $6.4&nbsp;million in property tax income, $2.7&nbsp;million of insurance policy fees, and $2.1&nbsp;million in income from servicing revenue and fees
received from referral of leases to third parties. In comparison, selected major components of other income for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 included $2.1&nbsp;million of insurance policy fees, and $1.5&nbsp;million in income from servicing
revenue and fees received from referral of leases to third parties. </P>

</TABLE> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The provision for credit losses increased $8.5&nbsp;million, or 43.6%, to $28.0&nbsp;million for the year
ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 from $19.5&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. Our provision for credit losses is charged against earnings to maintain our allowance at the appropriate level based on the projected probable net credit
losses inherent in our portfolio. Our projection of probable net credit losses incorporates a migration analysis, which is partially based on the delinquency status of the portfolio as of the measurement date, as well as consideration of multiple
qualitative factors. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The increase in our provision for credit losses was driven in part by higher delinquency experience in the portfolio
as of December&nbsp;31, 2019, resulting in a higher projection of expected credit losses. In addition, the increase in the provision was partially driven by replenishing the allowance from a higher <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">charge-off</FONT>
experience. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As of December&nbsp;31, 2019, delinquent accounts&nbsp;60&nbsp;days or more past due (as a percentage of minimum lease
payments receivable for leases and as a percentage of principal outstanding for loans) were 0.85%, compared to 0.65% at December&nbsp;31, 2018. This trend in higher delinquency experience is consistent with the trends for aging of receivables in the
equipment leasing industry, as published in the <I>Monthly Leasing and Finance Index </I>(<I><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">MLFI-25</FONT></I>) of the Equipment Leasing and Finance Association. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Net charge-offs were $22.4&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, compared to $18.3&nbsp;million for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2018. Net charge-offs as a percentage of average total finance receivables increased to 2.18% during the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, from 1.93% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. Industry data on average charge-offs
from <I><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">MLFI-25</FONT></I> indicates an 9.4% increase in net charge-offs as a percent of receivables for peers, while our increase in net <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">charge-off</FONT> percentage is 13.0%. Our
analysis of our higher <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">charge-off</FONT> experience indicates that the small business and lower credit quality borrowers in our portfolio were disproportionately impacted by the economic headwinds observed in 2019,
particularly in the second-half of the year. Both 2019 and 2018 include charge-offs related to fraudulent activity of single vendor partners (separate incidents) of $0.9&nbsp;million and $1.2&nbsp;million respectively. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Additional information regarding asset quality is included herein in the subsequent section, &#147;Finance Receivables and Asset
Quality.&#148; </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Provision for income taxes</I></B><I>. </I>Income tax expense of $9.7&nbsp;million was recorded for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2019, compared to an expense of $7.7&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. Our effective tax rate, which is a combination of federal and state income tax rates, was approximately 26.4% for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2019, compared to 23.6% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. The higher effective tax rate for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 is associated with changes in state statutory rates and related revaluation of deferred tax
as well as the increase of a valuation allowance against certain net operating loss carryforwards that are not expected to be utilized. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">-42- </P>

</DIV></Center>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Comparison of the Years Ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 and 2017 </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Net income</I></B><I>.</I> Net income of $25.0&nbsp;million was reported for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, resulting in diluted
earnings per share of $2.00, compared to net income of $25.3&nbsp;million and diluted earnings per share of $2.01 for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The comparable results are primarily due to an increase of $10.5&nbsp;million in interest
and fee income on a larger portfolio, an increase of $4.7&nbsp;million in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Non-Interest</FONT> income and a decrease of $1.2&nbsp;million in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Non-Interest</FONT> expense, offset by
increased interest expense of $6.2&nbsp;million primarily due to the impact on funding costs from the recent debt securitization and a net increase of $9.4&nbsp;million in tax expense primarily due to the revaluation of deferred tax assets and
liabilities in 2017 associated with the Tax Cut and Jobs Act of 2017 (the &#147;TCJA&#148;), offset by the lower Federal statutory rate in 2018 from the TCJA. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Return on average assets was 2.29% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, compared to a return of 2.59% for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2017. Return on average equity was 13.27% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, compared to a return of 15.38% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Overall, our average net investment in total finance receivables for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 increased 11.6% to
$944.6&nbsp;million, compared to $846.7&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. This change was primarily due to origination volume continuing to exceed lease repayments, asset sales and charge-offs. The <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">end-of-period</FONT></FONT> net investment in total finance receivables at December&nbsp;31, 2018 was $1.0&nbsp;billion, an increase of 9.4% from $914.4&nbsp;million at December&nbsp;31,
2017. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">During the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, we generated 33,105 new leases and loans in the amount of $704.9&nbsp;million,
compared to 32,189 new leases and loans in the amount of $629.4&nbsp;million originated for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. Approval rates increased from 56% at December&nbsp;31, 2017 to 57% at December&nbsp;31, 2018. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 compared to the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017, net interest and fee income increased
$4.4&nbsp;million, or 4.8%, primarily due to a $9.6&nbsp;million increase in interest income and a $0.9&nbsp;million increase in fee income offset by a $6.2&nbsp;million increase in interest expense. The provision for credit losses increased
$1.1&nbsp;million, or 6.0%, to $19.5&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 from $18.4&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017, due primarily to higher charge-offs attributed to growth in average finance receivables
and $1.2&nbsp;million in charge-offs during the fourth quarter due to fraudulent activity by a single vendor partner. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">-43- </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Net interest and fee income increased $4.4&nbsp;million, or 4.8%, to $95.5&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 from
$91.1&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The net interest and fee margin was 10.11% and 10.77% for the years ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 and December&nbsp;31, 2017, respectively. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Interest income, net of amortized initial direct costs and fees, increased $9.5&nbsp;million, or 10.9%, to $97.0&nbsp;million for the year
ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 from $87.5&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The increase in interest income was principally due to a 11.6% increase in average total finance receivables, which increased $97.9&nbsp;million to
$944.6&nbsp;million at December&nbsp;31, 2018 from $846.7&nbsp;million at December&nbsp;31, 2017. The increase in average total finance receivables was primarily due to origination volume continuing to exceed lease repayments. The weighted average
implicit interest rate on new finance receivables increased 47 basis point to 12.45% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, from 11.98% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Fee income increased $0.9&nbsp;million, or 6.0%, to $15.8&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 from $14.9&nbsp;million for
the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. Fee income included approximately $3.7&nbsp;million of net residual income for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 and $3.6&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Fee income also included approximately $9.3&nbsp;million in late fee income for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, which increased 3.3%,
compared to $9.0&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The increase in late fee income was primarily due to the increase in average total finance receivables. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Fee income, as a percentage of average total finance receivables, decreased 8 basis points to 1.68% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018
from 1.76% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. Late fees remained the largest component of fee income at 1.10% as a percentage of average total finance receivables for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, compared to 1.25% for the year
ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. As a percentage of average total finance receivables, net residual income was 0.44% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, compared to 0.50% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. </P>

 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Interest expense increased $6.2&nbsp;million to $17.4&nbsp;million, or 2.02% as a percentage
of average deposits, for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 from $11.2&nbsp;million, or 1.43% as a percentage of average deposits, for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The increase was almost equally due to increases in rate and average
balance of interest bearing liabilities. Interest expense, as an annualized percentage of average total finance receivables, increased 52 basis points to 1.84% for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, from 1.32% for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2017. The average balance of deposits was $785.6&nbsp;million and $777.7&nbsp;million for the years ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 and December&nbsp;31, 2017, respectively. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, average term securitizations outstanding were $75.2&nbsp;million at a weighted average coupon of
3.75%. There were no outstanding borrowings for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our wholly-owned subsidiary, MBB, serves as our
primary funding source. MBB raises time deposits through a variety of sources including: directly from customers, through the use of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">on-line</FONT> listing services, and through the use of deposit brokers. At
December&nbsp;31, 2018, brokered certificates of deposit represented approximately 56.3% of total deposits, while approximately 40.4% of total deposits were obtained from direct channels, and 3.3% were in the brokered MMDA Product. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Gain on Sale of Leases and Loans.</I></B><I> </I>Gain on sale of leases and loans increased $5.6&nbsp;million to $8.4&nbsp;million for
the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, from $2.8&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The increase in gain on sale was driven by an increase in assets sold which grew to $138.9&nbsp;million for 2018, compared to $66.7&nbsp;million
for 2017. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Insurance premiums written and earned.</I></B><I> </I>Insurance premiums written and earned increased $0.9&nbsp;million
to $8.1&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 from $7.2&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017, primarily due to an increase in the number of contracts enrolled in the insurance program as well as higher average
ticket size </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Other income.</I></B> Other income decreased $1.7&nbsp;million to $5.0&nbsp;million for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2018 from $6.7&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. Other income primarily includes various administrative transaction fees and fees received from referral of leases to third parties, and servicing income,
recognized as earned. Selected major components of other income for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 included $1.4&nbsp;million of referral income and servicing fees, and $2.1&nbsp;million of insurance policy fees. In comparison, selected major
components of other income for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017 included $3.4&nbsp;million of referral income and servicing income and $1.8&nbsp;million of insurance policy fees. </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Provision for credit losses. </I></B>The provision for credit losses increased $1.1&nbsp;million, or 6.0%, to $19.5&nbsp;million for the
year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 from $18.4&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The increase in our provision for credit losses resulted primarily from higher charge-offs due to growth in average finance receivables and
$1.2&nbsp;million in charge-offs during the fourth quarter due to fraudulent activity by a single vendor partner. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Net charge-offs were
$18.3&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, compared to $14.5&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The increase in charge-offs was primarily due to growth in average finance receivables and $1.2&nbsp;million in
charge-offs during the fourth quarter due to fraudulent activity by a single vendor partner. Net charge-offs as a percentage of average total finance receivables increased to 1.93% during the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, from 1.71% for the
year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The allowance for credit losses was $16.1&nbsp;million and $14.9&nbsp;million at December&nbsp;31, 2018 and December&nbsp;31, 2017, respectively. </P>

December&nbsp;31, 2018, compared to a benefit of $1.7&nbsp;million for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The increase was primarily due to the Company&#146;s revaluation of its deferred tax assets and liabilities at the new federal corporate

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman; " ALIGN="left">Equipment Finance consists of Equipment Finance Agreements, Installment Purchase Agreements, and other leases
and loans. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Net investments in leases and loans are generally <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">charged-off</FONT> when
they are contractually past due for 120&nbsp;days or more. Income recognition is discontinued on leases or loans when a default on monthly payment exists for a period of 90&nbsp;days or more. Income recognition resumes when a lease or loan becomes
less than 90&nbsp;days delinquent. At December&nbsp;31, 2019 and December&nbsp;31, 2018, there were no finance receivables past due 90 days or more and still accruing. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Working Capital Loans are generally placed in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-accrual</FONT> status when they are 30 days past due and <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">charged-off</FONT> at 60 days past due. The loan is removed from <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-accrual</FONT> status once sufficient payments are made to bring the loan current and reviewed by management. There were
no Working Capital Loans past due 30 days or more and still accruing. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Net charge-offs for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019 were
$22.4&nbsp;million, or 2.18% of average total finance receivables, compared to $18.3&nbsp;million, or 1.93% of average total finance receivables, for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018. Industry data on average charge-offs, as published in the
<I>Monthly Leasing and Finance Index </I>(<I><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">MLFI-25</FONT></I>) of the Equipment Leasing and Finance Association, indicates an 9.4% increase in net charge-offs as a percent of receivables for peers, while our
increase in net <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">charge-off</FONT> percentage is 13.0%. Our analysis of our higher <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">charge-off</FONT> experience indicates that the small business and lower credit quality borrowers in
our portfolio were disproportionately impacted by the economic headwinds observed in 2019, particularly in the second-half of the year. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Net charge-offs for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 were $18.3&nbsp;million, or 1.93% of average total finance receivables, compared to
$14.5&nbsp;million, or 1.71% of average total finance receivables, for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2017. The increase in charge-offs was primarily due to growth in average total finance receivables and $1.2&nbsp;million in charge-offs during
the fourth quarter due to fraudulent activity by a single vendor partner. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Lease portfolio losses tend to follow patterns based on the mix
of origination vintages comprising the portfolio. The timing of credit losses from the inception of a particular lease origination vintage to <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">charge-off</FONT> </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">-51- </P>

 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">
generally follows a pattern of lower losses for the first few months, followed by increased losses in subsequent months, then lower losses during the later periods of the lease term. Therefore,
the seasoning, or mix of origination vintages, of the portfolio affects the timing and amount of charge-offs. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Delinquent
accounts&nbsp;60&nbsp;days or more past due (as a percentage of minimum lease payments receivable for leases and as a percentage of principal outstanding for loans) were 0.85% at December&nbsp;31, 2019, 0.65% at December&nbsp;31, 2018 and 0.55% at
December&nbsp;31, 2017. This trend in higher delinquency experience is consistent with the trends for aging of receivables in the equipment leasing industry, as published in the<I> <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">MLFI-25</FONT></I>. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We maintain an allowance for credit losses at an amount sufficient to absorb losses inherent in our existing lease and loan portfolios as of
the reporting dates based on our projection of probable net credit losses. The factors and trends discussed above were included in the Company&#146;s analysis to determine its allowance for credit losses. (See &#147;<I>&#151;Critical Accounting
Policies</I>.&#148;) In addition, see <I>&#147;&#151;Adoption of accounting change for credit losses effective in 2020&#151;&#147;CECL&#148;</I>&#148; for discussion of changes effective January&nbsp;1, 2020 to our allowance measurement due to the
adoption of a new accounting standard. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Residual Performance </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our leases offer our end user customers the option to own the equipment at lease expiration. As of December&nbsp;31, 2019, approximately 55% of
our leases were one dollar purchase option leases, 44% were fair market value leases and less than 1% were fixed purchase option leases, the latter of which typically contain an
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">end-of-term</FONT></FONT> purchase option equal to 10% of the original equipment cost. As of December&nbsp;31, 2019, there were $29.3&nbsp;million of residual assets retained on our
Consolidated Balance Sheet, of which $23.4&nbsp;million, or 79.7%, were related to copiers. As of December&nbsp;31, 2018, there were $27.6&nbsp;million of residual assets retained on our Consolidated Balance Sheet, of which $23.6&nbsp;million, or
85.4%, were related to copiers. No other group of equipment represented more than 10% of equipment residuals as of December&nbsp;31, 2019 and 2018, respectively. Improvements in technology and other market changes, particularly in copiers, could
adversely impact our ability to realize the recorded residual values of this equipment. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Fee income included approximately
$3.7&nbsp;million, $3.7&nbsp;million and $3.6&nbsp;million of net residual income for the years ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively. Net residual income includes income from lease renewals and gains and losses on the
realization of residual values of leased equipment disposed at the end of term as further described below. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our leases generally include
renewal provisions and many leases continue beyond their initial contractual term. Based on the Company&#146;s experience, the amount of ultimate realization of the residual value tends to relate more to the customer&#146;s election at the end of
the lease term to enter into a renewal period, purchase the leased equipment or return the leased equipment than it does to the equipment type. We consider renewal income a component of residual performance. Renewal income, net of depreciation,
totaled approximately $5.5&nbsp;million, $5.0&nbsp;million and $4.7&nbsp;million for the years ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, the net loss on residual values disposed at end of term totaled $1.8&nbsp;million compared to a net
loss of $1.2&nbsp;million and $1.1&nbsp;million for the years ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 and December&nbsp;31, 2017, respectively. The primary driver of the changes was a shift in the mix of the amounts, types of disposition and age of equipment
disposed at the end of the applicable lease term. Historically and currently, our net residual income has exceeded 100% of the residual recorded on such leases. Management performs reviews of the estimated residual values and historical realization
statistics no less frequently than quarterly. There was no impairment recognized on estimated residual values during the years ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively. </P>

activity increased for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2019, and we sold $310.4&nbsp;million of assets that generated an immediate net <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">pre-tax</FONT> gain on sale of $22.2&nbsp;million. In comparison, for the year
ended December&nbsp;31, 2018, we sold $139.0&nbsp;million of assets for <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">pre-tax</FONT> gain on sale of $8.4&nbsp;million. The increased syndication volumes in 2019 reflects our origination growth from the prior year,
as well as the full year of production of FFR, which was acquired in late 2018. Future levels of syndication volumes will depend on our current assessment of our balance sheet composition, the quality and eligibility of originated contracts versus
the requirements of our counterparties, and our ability to negotiate terms acceptable to us, among other factors. We continue to service the contracts sold, which allows us to maintain an ongoing relationship with these customers. As of
December&nbsp;31, 2019, we were servicing a loan and lease portfolio of approximately $340&nbsp;million for others. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We have

time without any ability for us to draw down additional amounts. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Federal Funds Line of Credit with Correspondent
Bank</I></B><I>.</I><B><I> </I></B>MBB has established a federal funds line of credit with a correspondent bank. This line allows for both selling and purchasing of federal funds. The amount that can be drawn against the line is limited to
$25.0&nbsp;million. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Federal Reserve Discount Window. </I></B>In addition, MBB has received approval to borrow from the Federal
Reserve Discount Window based on the amount of assets MBB chooses to pledge. MBB had $32.8&nbsp;million in unused, secured borrowing capacity at the Federal Reserve Discount Window, based on 35.6&nbsp;million of net investment in leases pledged at
December&nbsp;31, 2019. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Term Note Securitizations. </I></B>On July&nbsp;27, 2018 we completed a $201.7&nbsp;million asset-backed
term securitization. This transaction was Marlin&#146;s eleventh term securitization and its first since 2010. It provides the company with fixed-cost borrowing with the objective of diversifying its funding sources. As with all prior
securitizations, this transaction was recorded as an <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#147;on-balance</FONT> sheet&#148; transaction and the financing is recorded in long-term borrowings in the Consolidated Balance Sheet. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">At December&nbsp;31, 2019 outstanding term securitizations amounted to $76.6&nbsp;million with $151.2&nbsp;million outstanding at
December&nbsp;31, 2018. As of December&nbsp;31, 2019, $84.6&nbsp;million of minimum lease payments receivable and $6.9&nbsp;million of restricted interest-earning deposits are assigned as collateral for the term note securitization. </P>
